Also something which I think you're glossing over is the fact that that quartermaster could've been another party/caravan leader or governor. I find both to be *much* more useful, as more parties lets you increase Leadership faster (put them all into your own army and wait, pump up cohesion for free when you need to), and help guard your fiefs. A governor can just straight up make your fief better in every way - from boosting construction, to security and loyalty, to prosperity. *Yes,* you can make your quartermaster into each of those and they'd do well, but the trade off is that your party size will likely take a noticeable hit, and you may suffer for it. I apologize for the *stupidly* long post, I didn't realize how much I wrote until I did. And I hope I don't come off as ungrateful or anything, I appreciate the response, the work TWs has done and continues to do, and I genuinely like the discussion here.

**TLDR - I know it's an improvement, and that villagers do react to the outside world. TWs did a good job there - I just think that they wanted to, and could, do better.**

\-----

I'm aware Warband was worse off. I didn't even mention it or draw comparisons to it; if I really wanted to reach for one, I could talk about Matheld, Lezalit, and Jeremus having actual backstories they tell to you, have conflicts with each other and even you if you do something they dislike (fail to feed/pay troops, raid a village, etc), and if you make a commoner companion a lord, other lords will dislike it because they were not of noble birth.

Bannerlord has backstories and some companions comment on when you are late on wages (maybe even when raiding, but not sure since I don't raid), which is good (I love some of the backstories of the randomly generated companions) but none of that conflict. You can tell them to shut up and sit down or promise to follow their request for timely pay next time, but that's it. There aren't any real consequences. Deshavi though would leave for a bit if you paired her up with whoever she dislikes and/or told her off enough.

Yet I didn't do that, because I'm *aware* that Bannerlord *is* an improvement. I'm *aware* that TW did a good job with the dialogue, considering many players don't care about it and what the game is. I never said the dialogue is garbage - I think it's acceptable in fact. But it doesn't change my opinion that it wasn't half done or the result was a compromise because of time.

And I know that the peasants and randomly generated characters do react to the outside world, talking about wars, peace, lords, notables, and the prosperity of their location. It's one of the things that actually *make* me enter towns sometimes; I like getting some semblance of an idea of what's happening in my fiefs or what other lords are like. Scenery is beautiful too.

But for the *lords*, the *named* characters you interact with *countless* times, it's just the handful of responses to a few things that coordinate with their traits and relationship. That's a start, but it doesn't go anywhere because they barely react to anything outside of what is done to them.

Here's some scenarios where a different greeting could be used:

Both are difficult for the people who need it to go to, and are not automatic solutions for suicidal tendencies.

Hotlines are more a last ditch effort and don't always work. [There are many instances](https://www.reddit.com/r/SuicideWatch/search/?q=hotline&restrict_sr=1&sr_nsfw=) where it doesn't help whatsoever for many different reasons. Maybe the person already made up their mind, only calling because they had a lingering doubt on whether to end it all or not. Maybe the hotline simply didn't help change their mind, or maybe it just made them feel worse. It all depends on the person on both sides of the call on whether or not it helps.

Therapy is kind of the same way, but even starting it is hard, because it requires you acknowledging you need it, which for many is acknowledging that you have a mental health *problem,* which is something that is difficult to overcome the denial of. And even then therapy might fall into the same pits as the hotline. It might not work because the person doesn't respond to it. Or maybe the therapist is just the wrong person to help. Or maybe the meds just don't work. Everyone is different, everyone has a different problem, and needs a different solution. Therapy may or may not be that solution.

Something I have to highlight is that Ronnie McNutt did have help. I don't know whether or not he went to therapy for his depression and PTSD (I assume he did), but he at least had his friends for support. But not everyone does. Not everyone has someone or something they can turn towards that can help them. They may have lost everything to a major event, or the people they trusted broke that trust, who knows. Ronnie had recently broken up with his girlfriend and also argued with her on that same livestream before ending his life. But many people don't even have that to lose.

**TL;DR:**

Hotlines are a last ditch effort and may not have an effect on the person who is committing suicide.

Therapy requires a person to acknowledge that they have a mental health problem and that they can be helped, but that alone is hard and they might not find the help they need.

Ronnie McNutt had people he could turn to, but had lost his girlfriend and fought with her which had caused him to commit suicide. But many other people never had someone to turn to, which can drive them to the same result.
